newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: A funny old week in Austrian politics.
newsitem.headline: A funny old week in Austrian politics.

text.p: A week is a long time in politics, a statesman once said, and that has certainly rung true in Austria over the past seven days.
Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky emerged triumphant from a bitter battle with his conservative coalition partners on January 12 over the privatisation of one of Austria's major banks.

On Sunday, looking as though the world had been lifted from his shoulders, Vranitzky gave his last major news conference as government leader, having resigned on Saturday after 10 1/2 years in power during a turbulent period in Austrian history.
His going had none of the back-stabbing drama that characterised the demise of former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, but came as no less of a surprise to the nation.

Senior Social Democrat Heinz Fischer said Vranitzky was leaving because of no political crisis or scandal, nor was he being pushed: "He just believed it was better for the country and this point in time was optimal."

After weeks of squabbling, the coalition of Social Democrats and their junior partner, the People's Party, held a crisis meeting a week ago in a showdown over the privatisation of the country's second biggest bank, Creditanstalt-Bankverein.

After 11 hours of talks, Vranitzky announced Creditanstalt had been sold to Bank Austria, its favoured bidder, and not to an international consortium backed by the conservatives led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel.

Newspapers and commentators hailed the deal as a huge victory for Vranitzky, consolidating his control over the shaky coalition and repairing his standing in his party, which crashed to an all-time low in a European election last October.
He said on Sunday it was just after that bank sale debacle that he finally made up his mind to call it a day.
"I came to my final decision in the first half of the week," Vranitzky told reporters, whom he successfully wrong-footed over the timing of his departure.
He surprised Schuessel, who appeared visibly irritated that he had been told of Vranitzky's resignation just an hour before the official announcement.
After being described the loser in the Creditanstalt sale, Schuessel had to suffer the further humiliation of not being consulted over Vranitzky's departure.
From looking like an uncertain chancellor being bossed around by an unruly government partner, Vranitzky left the political scene dominant and in control, and all within a week.
He has handed over the levers of power to Finance Minister Viktor Klima, whose standing in a popularity poll this month just surpassed that of Vranitzky for the first time.
"It was probably also a tactical calculation to resign now and let Klima run with the advantage," the daily Neue Krone Zeitung said in an editorial.
Knowing when to go is one of those calculations facing any government leader who keeps being voted back into power and Vranitzky appeared to have got it right.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the only leader in Europe to have ruled longer than Vranitzky, remains relatively popular after 14 years though he too has problems with his coalition.

American presidents can serve a maximum eight years and commentators said former French president Francois Mitterrand would have been better off leaving after his first seven-year term rather than last out a second.

In Britain, political obituary writers said Thatcher's write-up in the history books would have shone had she quit after 10 years in office in 1989, two years after winning her third election victory, rather than be dumped by her own party.
It was her predecessor Harold Wilson who is often quoted as saying: "A week is a long time in politics."
